Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist widely known as the architect of the nuclear age. He made towering contributions to both theoretical and experimental physics — he built the world's first nuclear reactor, developed the theory of beta decay, co-developed the statistical mechanics of fermions, and won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on induced radioactivity.

His most famous single achievement was constructing Chicago Pile-1 under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago in 1942. This was the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, and it achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction ever created by human hands. He also developed the theory of beta decay in 1933, introducing the weak interaction — one of the four fundamental forces — and he named the neutrino, calling it "the little neutral one," after Wolfgang Pauli's hypothesized particle.

Fermi discovered that slow neutrons are far more effective than fast neutrons at inducing nuclear reactions, a finding that led to the discovery of nuclear fission itself. He co-developed Fermi-Dirac statistics, which describe how fermions — electrons, protons, and neutrons — distribute themselves across energy states. In fact, fermions are named after him.

During the Manhattan Project, he served as associate director of Los Alamos Laboratory, playing a central role in developing the first atomic bomb and the Trinity test. He is also remembered for formulating the Fermi paradox, perhaps the most elegant question in science: "Where is everybody?" It highlights the contradiction between the high statistical probability that extraterrestrial life exists and the complete absence of evidence for contact.

Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation provided the theoretical foundation for Fermi's nuclear reactors. He was a close collaborator with Paul Dirac on quantum statistics, and worked alongside Richard Feynman at Los Alamos during the Manhattan Project.
